_meta.description: Hand-curated collector car taxonomy with integrated search index, model descriptions, and alias classification. Covers Classic, Antique, Collector, and Enthusiast vehicles from 1906–2026. Schema aligned with search function architecture: Make > Model > Generation > Variant/Trim with body_style as distinguishable field.

schema_notes.search_hierarchy: Year > Make > Model > Generation > Variant/Body Style > Trim
schema_notes.generation_role: Parallel search entry point alongside Year. Captures collector slang like '1st gen', 'shark', 'chrome bump'.
schema_notes.body_style_role: Distinguishable trait at variant level. Significant value differentiator (e.g. convertible vs hardtop Hemi Cuda).

search_index_blobs.keyword_blob: Formal names, engine codes, years, body styles, trim names
search_index_blobs.nickname_blob: Collector slang, generation nicknames, enthusiast shorthand
search_index_blobs.association_blob: Cultural references, famous owners, race history, movie connections

schema_notes.popularity_score: 0-100. Seeded by make tier + era + alias density. Blue chip makes (Ferrari, Porsche, Shelby, Lamborghini) receive highest base scores.

stats.version_notes: v6.4 — Added International Harvester (Scout 80/800/II, Travelall, IH Pickup), Saab (96, 99, 900, 9000, 9-3, 9-5), Volvo (Amazon, 1800, 140, 240, 260, 480, 740/760, 850/V70R, C30). Full search index rebuilt with transmission brands. Orphaned gen 127 fixed. Listing index schema included.

editorial_scope.geography: Global — USA, Germany, UK, Italy, France, Japan, Sweden

generations.name: 308 GTB/GTS (1975–1985)
generations.engine_options: 3.0 L Colombo V8,2.9 L V8 Turbo
generations.description: The Ferrari 308 brought the mid-engine V8 formula to a wider audience. Penned by Pininfarina, it remains one of the most recognisable shapes in automotive history. QV examples with the four-valve head are the pick of the range.
The 964 was the first major redesign of the 911 since 1963, yet retained the air-cooled soul purists demand. The RS is one of the most coveted road cars of the era.

generations.name: Series 1 (1961–1968)
generations.description: Unveiled at Geneva in 1961, the E-Type caused a sensation. Enzo Ferrari reportedly called it the most beautiful car ever made. Flat-floor 3.8 roadsters command the highest premiums.

generations.name: First Gen (1964–1973)
generations.description: The original Mustang created the pony car class overnight. Fastbacks and Boss variants are the collector targets. Shelbys occupy a category of their own.

generations.name: Miura P400 (1966-1969)
generations.description: The Miura is widely considered the world's first supercar. Its transverse mid-mounted V12 and Bertone body set the template for every supercar that followed. SV is the definitive variant.

generations.name: W198 Gullwing (1954–1957)
generations.description: The 300SL was the first production car with fuel injection and the first with gullwing doors. Alloy-bodied examples — just 29 built — are the ultimate expression of the model.

generations.name: E30 M3 (1986–1991)
generations.engine_options: 2.3 L S14 I4,2.5 L S14 Evolution
generations.description: Built to homologate BMW for touring car racing, the E30 M3 is the purest driver's car BMW ever made. Sport Evolution examples are among the most coveted BMWs in existence.

generations.name: S30 (1969–1978)
generations.description: The S30 redefined what a sports car could be at its price point. Clean, light, and mechanically honest — early 240Zs are among the cleanest rising-star buys in the market.

generations.name: 250 GTO (1962–1964)
generations.description: The Ferrari 250 GTO is the most valuable road-racing car ever made. Built to compete in GT racing, just 39 were produced. Every example is individually documented and authenticated.

generations.name: 250 GT Lusso (1962–1964)
generations.description: The 250 GT Lusso is the grand touring companion to the GTO, penned by Pininfarina. Long-nosed and beautiful, it was Steve McQueen's personal car and represents the apex of 1960s Ferrari road car design.

generations.name: 275 GTB (1964–1968)
generations.description: The 275 GTB introduced independent rear suspension to Ferrari road cars. The four-cam GTB/4 variant is the most coveted, while the NART Spider is among the rarest open Ferraris ever built.

generations.name: 328 GTB/GTS (1985–1989)
generations.description: The 328 refined the 308 formula with a larger 3.2-litre engine and restyled bodywork. The last of the classic Pininfarina mid-engine V8 line before the 348, it is increasingly sought after as a usable classic.

generations.name: Testarossa (1984–1996)
generations.description: The Testarossa's straked side intakes made it the defining supercar silhouette of the 1980s. A genuine 180mph car, it was Ferrari's flagship for over a decade. Single-mirror early cars command significant premiums.

generations.name: F40 (1987–1992)
generations.description: Built to celebrate Ferrari's 40th anniversary, the F40 was the last car Enzo personally approved. With no driver aids, no carpets, and raw twin-turbo power, it remains the purest supercar of its era.

generations.name: F355 (1994–1999)
generations.description: The F355 revived Ferrari's fortunes with a spectacular 375bhp five-valve-per-cylinder V8 and sublime handling. The Spider with manual gearbox is the collector's choice.

generations.name: 365 GTB/4 Daytona (1968–1973)
generations.description: The Daytona was the last front-engined Ferrari supercar before the mid-engine era. Named unofficially after Ferrari's 1-2-3 finish at the 1967 Daytona 24 Hours, the Spider version is extraordinarily rare.

generations.name: 512 BB (1976–1984)
generations.description: The Berlinetta Boxer was Ferrari's first mid-engine 12-cylinder road car. Visually dramatic and mechanically complex, later fuel-injected 512 BBi examples are more reliable but the carburetted 512 BB is the purist's choice.

generations.name: Dino 246 (1969–1974)
generations.description: The Dino was Ferrari's first mid-engine road car. Never badged as a Ferrari during production, it is now fully accepted into the canon. The GTS Targa is increasingly preferred for open-air driving.

generations.name: 901/911 Original (1963–1973)
generations.engine_options: 2.0 L Flat-6,2.2 L Flat-6,2.4 L Flat-6
generations.description: The original long-hood 911 is the most historically significant sports car of the postwar era. Early 2.0-litre S models and the 1973 Carrera RS 2.7 represent the pinnacle. Rust and accident history are the primary concerns.

generations.name: 930 Turbo (1975–1989)
generations.description: The 930 Turbo was the fastest production car in the world when launched and earned a fearsome reputation. The early 3.0 cars are the most dramatic; the 3.3 is more manageable. Widowmaker is the nickname — earned.
The 993 was the last air-cooled 911 and is widely regarded as the finest. Its multi-link rear suspension transformed handling and the twin-turbo Turbo S is among the fastest cars of the decade.

generations.name: 356 Pre-A / A (1948-1959)
generations.engine_options: 1.1 L Flat-4,1.3 L Flat-4,1.6 L Flat-4
generations.description: The 356 is where Porsche began. Built initially from Volkswagen components, it evolved into a sophisticated sports car. The Speedster is the most iconic body style; pre-A coupes are the most historically significant.

generations.engine_options: 1.7 L Flat-4,2.0 L Flat-4,2.0 L Flat-6
generations.description: The mid-engine 914 was a joint Porsche-VW project and was derided on launch. Today the six-cylinder 914/6 is a legitimate collector car and even the four-cylinder cars have a dedicated following.

generations.name: 944 / 944 Turbo (1982-1989)
generations.engine_options: 2.5 L I4,2.7 L I4,3.0 L I4 Turbo
generations.description: The 944 was Porsche's volume seller in the 1980s. The Turbo is the driver's pick; the S2 has the largest naturally aspirated four ever fitted to a production car. Turbos with full service history are increasingly collectible.

The 959 was the most technically advanced road car of its era — sequential twin-turbos, all-wheel drive, adjustable suspension, and 450bhp. It previewed technology the industry took a decade to adopt.

generations.name: Boxster 986 (1996-2004)
generations.engine_options: 2.5 L Flat-6,2.7 L Flat-6,3.2 L Flat-6 S
generations.description: The 986 Boxster saved Porsche from bankruptcy and established mid-engine roadster credentials. The early 2.5 IMS bearing issue is the key concern; post-2000 cars with the upgraded bearing are more reliable.

generations.name: GT40 (1964–1969)
generations.description: Built to beat Ferrari at Le Mans, the GT40 succeeded with four consecutive overall victories 1966–1969. Road cars are among the most valuable American vehicles ever built. Continuation cars require careful authentication.

generations.name: Thunderbird 1st Gen (1955–1957)
generations.description: The original two-seat Thunderbird was Ford's response to the Corvette. Its 1955–57 run is the most collectible — the addition of rear seats in 1958 marked the end of the sports car era. Porthole hardtops are especially desirable.

generations.name: Bronco 1st Gen (1966–1977)
generations.description: The original Bronco is the most collectible American 4x4 of the postwar era. Compact, capable, and beautiful, unrestored examples with documentation command large premiums. Restomod builds are extremely active.

generations.name: Fairlane 500 / GT (1966-1967)
generations.description: The mid-size Fairlane was Ford's muscle car sleeper. The Cobra and GT variants with 390 and 428 cubic inch engines are the collector targets. Rarer than comparable Mustangs and often undervalued.

generations.name: C1 (1953–1962)
generations.description: The original Corvette launched America's sports car tradition. Early six-cylinder cars are historically important; the later fuel-injected V8 "fuelie" models are the performance icons. 1963 is the last C1 year.

generations.name: C2 Sting Ray (1963–1967)
generations.description: The split-window 1963 coupe is the most sought-after American production car of the 1960s. Big-block 427 cars are the performance icons. The hidden headlights and dramatic styling make this the definitive Corvette.

generations.name: C3 (1968–1982)
generations.description: The C3 was Corvette's longest production run. Early big-block cars are most valued; the 1969 L88 and ZL1 are among the rarest American performance cars. Later chrome-bumper cars are accessible entry points.

generations.name: Z/28 1st Gen (1967–1969)
generations.description: The first-generation Camaro Z/28 was built for Trans-Am racing homologation. The 302 cubic inch V8 revved to 7,000rpm and the car dominated its class. COPO 427 and ZL1 cars are the most valuable Camaros ever built.

generations.name: Chevelle SS 396 / 1st Gen (1964-1967)
generations.engine_options: 7.4 L LS6 V8,7.4 L LS5 V8
generations.description: The 1970 Chevelle SS 454 LS6 produced 450bhp and was the most powerful muscle car of its era. Matching-numbers LS6 cars are among the most valuable muscle cars. Documentation is essential for authentication.

generations.name: El Camino 1st Gen (1959-1960)
generations.description: The El Camino SS blends car comfort with truck utility. The SS 396 and SS 454 variants from 1968–72 are the collector targets. Rarer than comparable cars and often undervalued, they are one of the better muscle car values.

generations.name: Nova SS 2nd Gen (1966-1967)
generations.description: The Nova SS was the compact muscle car sleeper. Light weight combined with available big-block engines produced impressive performance. COPO Novas with L78 396s are the top tier.

generations.name: Bel Air 1st Gen (1950-1954)
generations.description: The Bel Air is the definitive American classic. The 1955–57 tri-five generation is the most collectible; the 1957 two-door hardtop and convertible command the highest premiums. Fuel-injected fuelie cars are the performance icons.

generations.name: Impala SS 1st Gen (1961-1964)
generations.description: The full-size Impala SS was the aspirational American car of the 1960s. Convertibles and 409 cubic inch cars are the most desirable. Later lowrider culture has given certain configurations additional cultural value.

generations.name: Charger B-Body (1966–1974)
generations.description: The 1968–70 Charger is the definitive American muscle car. The 1969 Charger 500 and Daytona with aero nose are the rarest. Hemi cars are the most valuable; numbers matching is essential.

generations.name: Challenger 1st Gen (1970–1974)
generations.description: The E-body Challenger is one of the most beautiful American muscle cars. The R/T and T/A variants are the collector targets. Hemi convertibles are extraordinarily rare and among the most valuable Chrysler products.

generations.name: Viper SR I (1992–2002)
generations.description: The original Viper was a throwback to the AC Cobra — massive engine, no driver aids, enormous grip. The RT/10 roadster launched in 1992; the GTS coupe followed in 1996 and dominated GT racing.

generations.name: Coronet R/T / Super Bee (1967-1970)
generations.description: The Coronet R/T was the muscle car for those who knew. Running beneath the radar of Charger and Challenger, R/T and Super Bee variants with 440 and Hemi power are undervalued collector cars.

generations.name: Barracuda A-Body 1st Gen (1964-1966)
generations.description: The Barracuda predates the Mustang by two weeks, making it technically the first pony car. The 1970–74 E-body cars are the collector icons — especially Hemi and convertible examples, which are exceptionally rare.

generations.name: Road Runner 1st Gen (1968-1970)
generations.description: The Road Runner was conceived as a no-frills muscle car — maximum performance at minimum cost. The 440 six-pack and Hemi versions are the collector targets. The cartoon branding adds cultural cachet.

generations.name: Superbird (1970)
generations.description: The Superbird was built for NASCAR homologation — 1,920 road cars to qualify the aero nose and towering wing. Richard Petty's signature model, it is among the most distinctive American muscle cars ever built.

generations.name: GTO 1st Gen (1964–1967)
generations.description: The GTO is the car that created the muscle car segment. John DeLorean's decision to stuff a big-block into the Tempino in 1964 changed American car culture. The Judge is the most recognisable variant.

generations.name: Firebird/Trans Am (1969–2002)
generations.description: The Trans Am is the definitive Pontiac performance car. The 1969 Trans Am, 1973 SD-455, and 1977 Bandit Special Edition are the collector benchmarks. The 1970 Firebird Formula is the driver's choice.

generations.name: Cobra 289 (1962–1965)
generations.description: The 289 Cobra is the original — AC Ace chassis, Ford small-block, Carroll Shelby's vision. Lighter and more nimble than the 427, it is the purist's Cobra. CSX numbers and authenticity documentation are paramount.

generations.name: Cobra 427 (1965–1967)
generations.description: The 427 Cobra is the apex of American muscle in British clothes. The S/C (Semi-Competition) is the most extreme road car, with just 53 built. Beware continuations — authentic CSX registry documentation is essential.

generations.name: E-Type Series 2 (1968–1971)
generations.description: The Series 2 introduced exposed headlights and US-spec safety bumpers. The 4.2-litre engine gives excellent usability. Series 2 values sit below S1 but the cars offer the same driving experience at lower entry cost.

generations.name: XK120 (1948–1954)
generations.description: The XK120 was the fastest production car in the world when launched in 1948, reaching 120mph. The alloy-bodied 1948–49 cars are the most valuable; the steel-bodied production cars are the accessible entry point.

generations.name: XK140 (1954–1957)
generations.description: The XK140 refined the XK120 with rack-and-pinion steering and more cabin space. The MC variants with C-Type cylinder head offer significantly improved performance.

generations.name: XK150 (1957–1961)
generations.description: The XK150 was the last of the XK series and the most refined. Disc brakes on all four wheels were standard — a first for a British sports car. The 3.8 S engine produces 265bhp and offers genuine performance.

generations.name: D-Type (1954–1957)
generations.description: The D-Type won Le Mans three consecutive times. Monocoque construction, aircraft-influenced design, and a dry-sump XK engine made it the most advanced sports racing car of its era. XKSS road versions are among the rarest Jaguars.

generations.name: XJ-S Pre-HE (1975-1981)
generations.description: The XJ-S replaced the E-Type and was initially unloved. Time has been kind — the V12 coupe is now a genuine GT classic. HE (High Efficiency) models from 1981 onward are the most usable; the final V12 convertibles the most desirable.

generations.name: DB5 (1963–1965)
generations.description: The DB5 is the most famous car in the world. Bond association aside, it is a genuinely excellent high-speed grand tourer. Vantage specification adds a meaningful mechanical premium; Shooting Brake conversions are extraordinary.

generations.name: DB6 (1965–1971)
generations.description: The DB6 refined the DB5 with improved aerodynamics and a better interior. The Volante convertible is particularly elegant. Prince Charles owns a famous converted-to-biofuel example.

generations.name: DB4 GT Zagato (1960–1963)
generations.description: Just 19 original DB4 GT Zagatos were built and all are accounted for. Combining the lightweight DB4 GT with Zagato's double-bubble aluminium body, they are among the most valuable British cars ever made.

generations.name: V8 Vantage (1977–1989)
generations.description: The V8 Vantage was the fastest British car of the 1970s and a brutal machine. With up to 550bhp in later specification, it rivalled Ferrari and Lamborghini. The Volante convertible is especially rare.

generations.name: W198 Roadster (1957–1963)
generations.description: The 300SL Roadster succeeded the Gullwing and offered more practical entry than the high sills demanded. Disc brakes arrived in 1961 and a Rudge alloy wheel option is particularly desirable.

generations.name: 190SL (1955–1963)
generations.description: The 190SL was the accessible companion to the 300SL, sharing the same classic styling at lower cost. A genuine two-seat roadster with a hard-top option, it is one of the most elegant Mercedes ever made.

generations.name: 280SL Pagoda (1963–1971)
generations.description: The Pagoda SL is one of the most beautiful Mercedes ever made. The concave hardtop gives the car its nickname. The 280SL is the most desirable variant; earlier 230 and 250SL cars offer lower entry cost.

generations.name: 450SEL 6.9 (1975–1980)
generations.description: The 450SEL 6.9 was the fastest four-door car in the world when launched. Hydropneumatic self-levelling suspension and a 286bhp engine made it the S-Class benchmark. The drivers' car of choice for Saudi royalty and racing drivers.

generations.name: 500E (1991–1994)
generations.description: The 500E was hand-assembled by Porsche — each car spent three days at Zuffenhausen. A 326bhp 5-litre V8 in a mid-size Mercedes, it remains the benchmark Q-car. Only 10,479 were built.

The 507 is one of the most beautiful cars of the 20th century. Designed by Albrecht von Goertz, only 252 were made. Elvis Presley owned two. BMW almost went bankrupt building it at a loss, leading to the company's near-sale.

generations.name: 2002 Turbo (1973–1974)
generations.description: The 2002 Turbo was Europe's first turbocharged production car. Aggressive reverse-stencilled bodywork and a distinctive spoiler made it instantly recognisable. Only 1,672 were made and most have survived.

generations.name: M1 (1978–1981)
generations.description: The M1 is BMW's only true mid-engine supercar. Designed by Giugiaro and built with help from Lamborghini, it competed in the one-make Procar series. The road car is rarer than many exotics and increasingly sought after.

generations.name: E28 M5 (1984–1988)
generations.description: The E28 M5 was the world's fastest production sedan when launched. Hand-built by BMW Motorsport with the M1's engine in a discreet sedan body — the original Q-car. Only 2,241 were made.

generations.name: E46 M3 (2000–2006)
generations.description: The E46 M3 is widely regarded as the finest M car BMW has made. The naturally aspirated S54 engine to 8,000rpm and hydraulic steering define the experience. CSL and GTR variants are the collector targets.

generations.name: Countach LP400 / LP400S (1974-1982)
generations.description: The Countach defined the supercar poster era. Bertone's impossibly dramatic wedge shape made every other car look ordinary. The LP400 "periscopio" is the purist's car; LP5000 QV the fastest. Wings are optional aesthetics.

generations.name: Diablo / VT (1990-1998)
generations.description: The Diablo succeeded the Countach and raised the supercar bar to 202mph. The Roadster is the rarest body style; the GT and GTR are the homologation specials. Audi ownership brought build quality improvements from 1998.

generations.name: Espada (1968–1978)
generations.description: The Espada is the only four-seat Lamborghini supercar. Bertone designed a genuinely beautiful 2+2 that could carry the family at 150mph. Three series were produced; Series III offers the most refinement.

generations.name: Jalpa (1981–1988)
generations.description: The Jalpa was Lamborghini's entry-level car in the 1980s and shared lineage with the Urraco and Silhouette. A genuine mid-engine V8 Targa for less than the price of a Countach — and now significantly undervalued.

generations.name: F1 (1992–1998)
generations.description: The McLaren F1 is the greatest driver's car ever made. Three-seat central driving position, naturally aspirated V12, carbon monocoque, and no traction control. It held the production car speed record for 14 years. GTR won Le Mans in 1995.

generations.name: Giulia Sprint GTA (1965–1969)
generations.description: The GTA (Gran Turismo Alleggerita) is the lightweight racing version of the Giulia Sprint. Aluminium bodywork, twin-plug head, and close-ratio gearbox. It dominated European Touring Car racing for years.

generations.name: Spider Duetto/Series 1 (1966–1969)
generations.description: The Series 1 Spider Duetto — round-tail design — is the most beautiful Alfa roadster. Made famous by The Graduate. Later series are more refined but the Duetto remains the collector target.

generations.name: Montreal (1970–1977)
generations.description: The Montreal combined Bertone styling with a detuned Formula 1 V8. Complex, temperamental, and magnificent — it is one of the most charismatic grand tourers of the 1970s and significantly undervalued.

generations.name: 33 Stradale (1967–1969)
generations.description: Only 18 were built. The 33 Stradale is widely considered the most beautiful car ever made. Franco Scaglione's body over the Type 33 racing chassis resulted in a road car of extraordinary rarity and beauty.

generations.name: Type 35 (1924–1931)
generations.description: The Type 35 is the most successful racing car in history, with over 2,000 race victories. Ettore Bugatti's masterpiece combined engineering and artistry. The supercharged 35B and 35C are the most powerful variants.

generations.name: Type 57 (1934–1940)
generations.description: The Type 57 is the pinnacle of pre-war grand touring. The Atlantic coupe, with just four originals built, is the most valuable car in existence. Jean Bugatti designed the body; the engine is pure Ettore.

generations.name: EB110 (1991–1995)
generations.description: Built to revive Bugatti, the EB110 was a technological tour de force — 60-valve quad-turbo V12, all-wheel drive, carbon chassis. Michael Schumacher owned one. The company went bankrupt before reaching its potential.

generations.name: Stratos (1973–1978)
generations.description: The Stratos is the most purpose-built rally car ever made road-legal. Using the Ferrari Dino V6, it won the World Rally Championship three consecutive times. The road car is essentially a homologation device.

generations.name: Delta Integrale (1987–1994)
generations.description: The Lancia Delta HF Integrale is the definitive homologation supercar of the 1980s and early 1990s. Six consecutive WRC Manufacturers' Championships from 1987 to 1992 give it a competition record unmatched in rallying history. The road cars are direct descendants of the rally machines -- turbocharged 2.0-litre four-cylinder, four-wheel drive, and a chassis tuned by Abarth engineers. The Integrale 8V is the raw original; the 16V gains power and composure; the Evo I sharpened the aerodynamics with flared arches; and the Evo II is the ultimate road specification with 215 bhp and the widest bodywork. The Finale Edizione -- 250 in five colours -- is the last and most collectible of all. Rust is the enemy; documented, rust-free examples command strong and rising premiums.

The 037 was the last rear-wheel drive car to win the WRC. Built around a central monocoque with a supercharged engine behind the driver, it defeated the Quattro on loose surfaces. Road cars are homologation specials.

generations.name: 2000GT (1967–1970)
generations.description: The Toyota 2000GT is Japan's first supercar and among the most beautiful cars of the 1960s. Only 351 were built; the two open-top Bond Girl cars are unique. Yamaha developed the twin-cam engine.

generations.name: Supra A80 (1993–2002)
generations.description: The A80 Supra with twin-turbo 2JZ engine is the most tuneable sports car ever made. Standard cars produce 320bhp but the engine can be taken to 1,000bhp on stock internals. Pure manual TT examples command significant premiums.

generations.name: FJ40 Land Cruiser (1960–1984)
generations.description: The FJ40 is the most iconic Land Cruiser and one of the most collectable 4x4s. Simple, unstoppable, and endlessly restorable. Clean examples are increasingly rare as the restomod movement devours survivors.

generations.name: Skyline GT-R R32 (1989–1994)
generations.description: The R32 GT-R ended BMW M3 dominance in touring car racing so comprehensively it was nicknamed Godzilla. AWD, twin-turbo RB26, and ATTESA E-TS AWD. Increasingly valuable and Japan is now releasing export approvals.

generations.name: Skyline GT-R R34 (1999–2002)
generations.description: The R34 GT-R is the most iconic Japanese car ever made. Paul Walker's Supra competitor in Fast and Furious. Only 11,578 were built and only now becoming legal to import to the US under 25-year rule.

generations.name: 300ZX Twin Turbo Z32 (1990–1996)
generations.description: The Z32 300ZX Twin Turbo was faster than the Ferrari 348 in contemporary tests. Japanese manufacturers' horsepower agreement limited it to 300ps officially — actual output was higher. The 2+2 sacrifices little to the 2-seater.

generations.name: Cosmo 110S (1967–1972)
generations.description: The Cosmo 110S was the world's first twin-rotor production car. Mazda's first sports car, it debuted rotary technology that would define the brand for 50 years. Series I cars from 1967–68 are the most desirable.

generations.name: RX-7 FB (1978–1985)
generations.description: The first-generation RX-7 is the purest rotary sports car. Light, balanced, and beautiful, the FB rewards the enthusiast driver. Turbo models are the performance pick; GSL-SE the touring choice.

generations.name: RX-7 FD (1991–2002)
generations.description: The FD RX-7 is the definitive Mazda sports car. Sequential twin turbos, near-perfect weight distribution, and extraordinary chassis dynamics. Apex seal reliability improved in later production. A modern classic.

generations.name: Beetle Type 1 (1938–2003)
generations.engine_options: 1.1 L Flat-4,1.2 L Flat-4,1.5 L Flat-4,1.6 L Flat-4
generations.description: The most produced car in history. Pre-1967 oval-window and split-window bugs are the collector targets. Cabriolets are desirable in all years. Cal-look and Baja builds are distinct collectible sub-cultures.

generations.name: Golf GTI Mk1 (1976–1983)
generations.description: The original Golf GTI invented the hot hatch genre. Simple, light, and fun — it combined everyday practicality with genuine driving pleasure. Campaign and Pirelli special editions are the collector targets.

generations.name: Karmann Ghia (1955–1974)
generations.engine_options: 1.2 L Flat-4,1.5 L Flat-4,1.6 L Flat-4
generations.description: The Karmann Ghia combined VW Beetle mechanicals with an Italian-influenced body by Ghia and coachbuilt quality from Karmann. Convertibles are the most desirable; early 1955–59 models with the larger rear window command premiums.

generations.name: NSX NA1 (1990–2005)
generations.description: The NSX was designed with Ayrton Senna's input and proved a naturally aspirated V6 could deliver supercar performance with daily reliability. Manual Type S and Type R variants are the collector targets.

generations.name: P1800 (1961–1973)
generations.description: The P1800 is Volvo's sports car — made famous by Roger Moore in The Saint. The 1800ES shooting brake of 1971–73 is increasingly sought after. Irv Gordon's example holds the world record for highest mileage.

generations.name: DS (1955–1975)
generations.description: The DS was 15 years ahead of its time. Hydropneumatic suspension, disc brakes, and space-age styling revolutionised what a car could be. The presidential Cabriolet is the rarest variant; Décapotable conversions are exceptional.

generations.name: SM (1970–1975)
generations.engine_options: 2.7 L Maserati V6,3.0 L Maserati V6
generations.description: The SM combined Citroën's hydropneumatic sophistication with a Maserati V6 — the most exotic French car ever made. Self-centring power steering and an extraordinary ride. Complexity rewards patience.

generations.name: 2CV (1948–1990)
generations.description: The 2CV was designed to put France on wheels — minimum cost, maximum practicality. The Charleston and Dolly special editions are the collector picks. The Sahara with two engines is extraordinarily rare.

generations.name: 500 Nuova (1957–1975)
generations.description: The Nuova 500 is Italy's answer to the Mini — the car that mobilised a nation. The Abarth 595 and 695 variants are serious performance cars in a tiny package. Giardiniera estate versions are remarkably practical.

generations.name: 124 Spider (1966–1985)
generations.description: The 124 Spider is the most successful Italian roadster ever made. Pininfarina bodywork over a capable twin-cam platform. Abarth-prepared versions competed successfully in rallying.

generations.name: Fiat Dino (1966–1973)
generations.description: The Fiat Dino used a shared Ferrari Dino V6 engine — produced by Fiat to meet Ferrari's homologation requirement. The 2.4 Spider is the most desirable; the coupe by Bertone is equally beautiful.

generations.name: Series I (1948–1958)
generations.description: The original Land Rover established the template for the utilitarian 4x4. Early 80-inch cars are the most historic; 86 and 88-inch models are more usable. Centre-steer prototypes exist but were never produced.

generations.name: Series II/IIA (1958–1971)
generations.description: The Series II refined the original with a wider track and more powerful engine. The IIA introduced the 2.25-litre engine that defined Land Rovers for decades. Station Wagon examples are the most usable.

generations.name: Defender 90/110 (1983–2016)
generations.description: The Defender is the most capable production 4x4 ever made. Final year 2015 cars command premiums; early 90s V8s are sought after for restomods. Heritage-spec and SVX limited editions are collector targets.

generations.name: Pantera (1971–1992)
generations.description: The Pantera combined Italian styling with American Ford V8 muscle. Sold through Ford dealers in the US, it was affordable supercar ownership. GTS and GT5-S variants are the performance picks. Elvis Presley shot his.

generations.name: Mangusta (1967–1971)
generations.engine_options: 4.7 L Ford V8,5.0 L Ford V8
generations.description: The Mangusta (Italian for mongoose — mongoose beats cobra) was designed as a Shelby Cobra killer. Giugiaro styled it with iconic butterfly engine covers. Only 401 were made and the handling is challenging.

generations.name: Elan (1962–1975)
generations.description: The Elan defined the lightweight British sports car. Colin Chapman's backbone chassis and fibreglass body produced a roadster of extraordinary agility. The Sprint is the ultimate development; the +2 the practical choice.

generations.name: Esprit S1-S3 / Turbo (1976-1987)
generations.engine_options: 2.0 L Turbo I4,3.5 L Twin-Turbo V8
generations.description: The Esprit Turbo was a proper supercar in a Giugiaro suit. The V8 GT of 1996 onward raised performance to match Ferrari. The white S1 from The Spy Who Loved Me is the cultural icon.

generations.name: Elise S1 (1996-2000)
generations.description: The S1 Elise reset expectations for what a lightweight sports car could be. Extruded aluminium chassis, sub-700kg weight, and telepathic handling. The 111S is the performance variant; standard cars are the driving purist's choice.

generations.name: AMX 1st Gen (1968-1970)
generations.description: The AMX was AMC's two-seat muscle car — one of only three true two-seat American production cars alongside the Cobra and Corvette. The 390 and Go Package variants are the collector targets.

generations.name: Javelin 1st Gen (1968-1970)
generations.description: The Javelin was AMC's pony car challenger. The Trans-Am racing programme produced real performance hardware. Pierre Cardin and Hurst editions stand out. Often overlooked relative to Mustang and Camaro.

generations.name: Eldorado Biarritz (1953-1958)
generations.description: The Eldorado name ran from 1953 to 2002 across radically different cars. The 1953 Eldorado is among the finest American convertibles. The 1967 front-wheel drive Eldorado pioneered the personal luxury segment.

generations.name: Allante (1987–1993)
generations.engine_options: 4.1 L V8,4.5 L V8,4.6 L Northstar V8
generations.description: The Allante was flown Pininfarina bodies from Italy for assembly in Detroit. The final 1993 Northstar engine transformed the car. Regarded as a failure at launch, quality 1993 examples are now undervalued.

generations.name: 442 1st Gen (1964-1967)
generations.description: 4-4-2 stood for four-barrel carb, four-speed gearbox, dual exhausts. The W-30 and W-32 performance packages are the collector targets. Hurst/Olds editions are particularly desirable.

generations.name: Toronado 1st Gen (1966-1970)
generations.description: The 1966 Toronado was the first American front-wheel drive car since the Cord 810. The styling by David North is dramatic and forward-looking. The 1966–67 cars are the collector targets.

generations.name: Gran Sport (1965–1975)
generations.description: The Buick Gran Sport, especially the Stage 1 455, is the most underrated muscle car of its era. The 455 Stage 1 produced more torque than any contemporary V8. Skylark GS 455 Stage 1 examples are significantly undervalued.

generations.name: Riviera 1st Gen (1963-1965)
generations.description: Bill Mitchell's 1963 Riviera is considered the finest American design of the postwar era. The combination of Rolls-Royce-inspired lines with American V8 power set a template for the personal luxury coupe segment.

generations.name: Ghibli 1st Gen (1966–1973)
generations.description: The Ghibli is the most beautiful Maserati ever made — Giorgetto Giugiaro's masterpiece for the company. The Spyder is exceptionally rare at 125 built. A 4.9 SS example is among the most desirable Italian cars of its era.

generations.name: Bora (1971–1978)
generations.description: The Bora was Maserati's first mid-engine road car, designed by Giugiaro and featuring a Citroën hydraulic system. Shares architecture with the Merak. The 4.9 variant is more powerful and the collector preference.

generations.name: Merak (1972–1983)
generations.description: The Merak shared the Bora's body and mid-engine layout but used a smaller V6. The SS variant is the most desirable. Citroën hydraulics can be complex but the cars are rewarding when properly sorted.

generations.name: 3500 GT (1957-1961)
generations.description: The 3500 GT was Maserati's first real production car and established the company as a grand touring manufacturer. The Spyder is far rarer than the coupe; Vignale-bodied examples are especially collectible.

generations.name: Lancer Evolution VI (1999–2001)
generations.description: The Evo VI Tommi Mäkinen Edition is the most desirable Lancer Evolution. Built to celebrate four consecutive WRC driver titles, it features a titanium turbo and front-facing fog lights. TME examples command significant premiums.

generations.name: 3000GT VR-4 (1990–1999)
generations.description: The 3000GT VR-4 was the most technically complex Japanese sports car of its era — active aerodynamics, all-wheel drive, all-wheel steering, and twin turbos. The Spyder convertible is exceptionally rare.

generations.name: Impreza WRX STI GC8 (1994–2000)
generations.description: The GC8 STI is the rally homologation hero. Colin McRae and Richard Burns won WRC titles in cars based on this platform. Version VI and RA-R examples are the collector targets. Right-hand drive import demand is growing.

generations.name: TR3A (1957-1962)
generations.description: The TR3A was the first British production car with disc brakes and the first to offer them as standard. Simple, tough, and rewarding, it dominated American sports car racing in the late 1950s.

generations.name: TR6 (1969–1976)
generations.description: The TR6 is the last of the traditional Triumph roadsters. Karmann-styled with a 150bhp straight-six, it remains one of the most accessible British classic sports cars. US-spec fuel injection cars need upgrading.

generations.name: Stag (1970–1977)
generations.description: The Stag had one of the most beautiful bodies of any 1970s car. The V8 engine's cooling issues are legendary but modern fixes make them reliable. Well-maintained examples are among the most usable British classics.

generations.name: MGA 1500 / Twin Cam (1955-1959)
generations.description: The MGA replaced the boxy T-series with a modern aerodynamic body. The Twin Cam is the performance variant — complex but rewarding when right. The 1600 Mk II is the most usable standard car.

generations.name: MGB (1962-1974)
generations.description: The MGB is the world's most successful British sports car. Monocoque construction, good performance, and affordable parts make it the ideal introduction to classic motoring. Rubber-bumper cars are cheapest; chrome-bumper most desirable.

generations.name: MG TD (1949–1953)
generations.description: The TD was the first MG designed for left-hand drive and the car that established the MG brand in America. Independent front suspension improved the T-series chassis. The TF that followed is more refined but rarer.

generations.name: 3000 Mk III (1963-1967)
generations.description: The 3000 Mk III is the finest of the Big Healeys. The Phase II interior with wood dashboard and twin SU carburettors producing 148bhp. Rally-proven and genuinely fast, these are among the most usable classic British sports cars.

generations.name: Sprite Mk I (1958–1961)
generations.description: The Frogeye Sprite is the most endearing British sports car. Fixed headlights in the bonnet, no external boot opening, and minimal equipment — just driving pleasure. Shared Bugeye DNA with early Midgets.

generations.name: Grifo (1963–1974)
generations.engine_options: 5.4 L Chevrolet V8,6.5 L Chevrolet V8,5.8 L Ford V8
generations.description: The Iso Grifo combined Bertone styling with American V8 reliability. Giotto Bizzarrini's chassis gave it handling to match the Ferrari 275 GTB. The Can Am Series II with 7-litre Corvette engine is the most brutal variant.

generations.name: Rivolta (1962–1970)
generations.description: The Iso Rivolta is the grand touring companion to the Grifo. Bertone's four-seat body over the same Bizzarrini chassis offers comfort without sacrificing the V8 character. Significantly undervalued relative to Italian competitors.

generations.name: Avanti (1963–1964)
generations.description: Raymond Loewy designed the Avanti as a last-ditch attempt to save Studebaker. The supercharged R3 broke 29 land speed records. After Studebaker closed, the design continued under Avanti Motor Corporation.

generations.name: Sonett III (1970–1974)
generations.description: The Sonett III was Saab's last attempt at a sports car. Styled by Sergio Coggiola with a fibreglass body, it used a Ford Taunus V4 engine. The rarest and most refined of the Sonett series.

generations.name: R-Type Continental (1952–1955)
generations.description: The R-Type Continental was the fastest four-seat car in the world in 1952. H.J. Mulliner's fastback body is a masterpiece of elegant engineering. Only 208 were built and all are documented.

generations.name: Le Mans Replica (1948–1953)
generations.description: The Frazer Nash Le Mans Replica is the ultimate expression of chain-drive sports car engineering. Just 34 were built with Bristol engines. These cars finished 3rd overall at Le Mans in 1949.

generations.name: J2 (1950–1952)
generations.description: The Allard J2 was the Cobra before the Cobra — massive American V8 in a lightweight British roadster. Sydney Allard drove one to third overall at Le Mans in 1950. A direct inspiration for Carroll Shelby.

generations.name: 4½ Litre Blower (1929–1931)
generations.description: The Blower Bentley is the most famous pre-war British racing car. Birkin's supercharger was opposed by W.O. Bentley himself. Among the most desirable cars ever made.

generations.name: 550 Spyder (1953–1956)
generations.description: The 550 Spyder is one of the most significant racing cars Porsche ever built. James Dean died in his on September 30, 1955 — serial number 550-0055. Lightweight, mid-engine, and devastatingly effective against far more powerful machinery.

generations.name: 718 Spyder (1960–1962)
generations.description: The 718 RSK and RS60/RS61 were Porsche's factory weapons at Le Mans, Targa Florio, and the Nürburgring. Stirling Moss drove them to numerous victories. Fewer than 22 were built and all are accounted for.

The 912 used the 911 body with an economical four-cylinder engine from the 356. Originally dismissed as a lesser 911, early short-wheelbase examples are now recognised as pure, lightweight driving machines. The rare 912E of 1976 used a VW engine.

generations.name: 911 SC (1978–1983)
generations.description: The 911 SC is the most overlooked classic 911. Reliable, sorted, and driving beautifully — it benefits from decades of development without the premiums of the Carrera 3.2. The Cabriolet of 1983 was the first open 911 since the 356. An undervalued entry point.

generations.name: 911 Carrera 3.2 (1984–1989)
generations.description: The 3.2 Carrera was the final evolution of the original 911 before the 964. Bosch Motronic fuel injection, G50 gearbox from 1987, and the best balance of old-school character with modern reliability. Club Sport and Speedster variants are the collector targets.

The 924 was Porsche's entry-level car and initially derided for its VW/Audi origins. The 924 Turbo is a genuine performance car; the 924 Carrera GT and GTS are homologation specials of extraordinary rarity. Le Mans class winners.

generations.name: 928 S / S4 (1978-1991)
generations.description: The 928 was Ferdinand Piëch's vision of a 911 successor — front-engine V8 grand tourer. It never replaced the 911 but earned a devoted following. The GTS is the definitive final variant. Originally driven by Tom Cruise in Risky Business.

The 968 was the final development of the 944/924 lineage — lighter, faster, and better in every way. Its 3.0-litre four-cylinder was the largest naturally aspirated four in any production car. Club Sport is the driver's car; Cabriolet the rarest.

generations.name: 996 GT3 (1999–2005)
generations.description: The 996 GT3 introduced the Metzger engine — a motorsport-derived unit shared with the GT1 racer. Despised initially for the water-cooled transition, the GT3 is now recognised as a superb driver's car. The RS variants are the collector targets.

generations.name: 993 GT2 (1995–1997)
generations.description: The 993 GT2 is the most extreme road car Porsche made in the air-cooled era. Rear-wheel drive, twin-turbocharged, 430bhp, and stripped for racing homologation. Just 194 road cars were built. The ultimate air-cooled Porsche.

generations.name: Carrera GT (2004–2006)
generations.description: The Carrera GT used a Formula 1-derived V10 and a ceramic clutch that earned a fearsome reputation. Paul Walker died in one in 2013, intensifying its cultural notoriety. Carbon monocoque, pushrod suspension — pure racing car technology on the road.

generations.name: Skyline GT-R R33 (1995–1998)
generations.description: The R33 GT-R is the bridge between the legendary R32 and the iconic R34. Often overlooked, it is the most driver-friendly of the trio — wider track, better balanced, and increasingly undervalued. BCNR33 V-Spec examples are the collector targets.

generations.name: S2000 (1999–2009)
generations.description: The S2000 was Honda's 50th anniversary car and possibly the finest front-engine, rear-drive roadster ever made. The 9,000rpm F20C engine is a masterpiece. AP1 with the high-revving 240bhp engine is the enthusiast pick; AP2 more usable.

generations.name: NSX Type R (NA2)
generations.description: The NA2 NSX-R is the ultimate expression of the original NSX. Weight reduced by over 100kg through extensive use of carbon and titanium. Forged pistons, close-ratio gearbox, high-downforce bodywork. Only 200 were made for the Japanese domestic market.

generations.name: Celica GT-Four ST205 (1994–1999)
generations.description: The ST205 Celica GT-Four was Toyota's WRC homologation weapon. Carlos Sainz and Didier Auriol drove it to titles. The road car repackaged full rally hardware — all-wheel drive, intercooled turbo, and limited-slip differentials — in a practical coupe.

generations.name: MX-5 NA Miata (1989–1997)
generations.engine_options: 1.6 L B6 I4,1.8 L BP I4
generations.description: The original Miata revived the lightweight British roadster formula with Japanese reliability. Colin Chapman's ghost in a Mazda badge. Simple, balanced, and joyful — the most raced production car in history. Special editions and low-mileage survivors command premiums.

generations.name: MX-5 NB (1998–2005)
generations.engine_options: 1.8 L BP I4,1.8 L BP Turbo
generations.description: The NB refined the NA formula with a crisper body and optional power-retractable hardtop. The Mazdaspeed Miata turbocharged version is the performance pick. NB2 facelift cars with revised headlights are the most desirable.

generations.name: Integra Type R DC5 (2001–2006)
generations.description: The DC5 Type R is arguably the greatest front-wheel drive car ever made. The K20A engine to 8,400rpm, close-ratio six-speed, helical limited-slip differential, and weight trimmed to the bone. Championship White examples are the collector standard.

generations.name: MR2 Spyder W30 (1999–2007)
generations.description: The W30 MR2 Spyder is the mid-engine roadster Lotus could never quite make affordable. Light, balanced, and tossable — the VVTL-i engine variant is the performance pick. Rising sharply as buyers discover what Miata money can get in mid-engine form.

generations.name: Ferrari 360 Modena (1999–2005)
generations.description: The 360 Modena was Ferrari's first all-aluminium production car and a quantum leap from the F355 it replaced. Pininfarina's body is more dramatic; the 400bhp V8 more tractable. The Challenge Stradale is the stripped track variant; Spider the open-air choice.

generations.name: Ferrari 430 Scuderia (2007–2009)
generations.description: The 430 Scuderia stripped the F430 to its essentials — 100kg lighter, 510bhp, carbon ceramic brakes, and the E-Diff from the 430 Challenge. The Scuderia Spider 16M followed in 2009. Just 499 of each built. The benchmark lightweight Ferrari of its era.

generations.name: Ferrari Enzo (2002–2004)
generations.description: Named after the founder, the Enzo applied Formula 1 technology directly to a road car — carbon fibre body, semi-automatic transmission, carbon ceramic brakes, active aerodynamics. 400 were planned; 399 sold through Ferrari's client list, one donated to the Vatican.

generations.name: Gallardo (2003–2013)
generations.description: The Gallardo became Lamborghini's best-selling car of all time — and proved the company could build a reliable, usable supercar. The LP570-4 Superleggera is the driver's pick; the Spyder Performante the open-air choice. Now approaching the bottom of their depreciation curve.

generations.name: Murciélago (2001–2010)
generations.description: The Murciélago was the last Lamborghini developed entirely without Audi's influence. Its 6.5-litre V12 in the LP670 produces 670bhp with minimal electronic intervention. The LP670-4 SuperVeloce is the ultimate expression — just 350 built.

generations.name: V8 Vantage (2005–2018)
generations.description: The modern V8 Vantage is the purest Aston Martin of the recent era. Manual gearbox, front-engine rear-drive, beautiful proportions, and a sonorous V8. The 4.7-litre N430 and GT8 variants are the enthusiast picks. Among the most usable modern classics.

generations.name: Vanquish Mk1 (2001–2007)
generations.description: The original Vanquish was Aston Martin's hand-built flagship — a 190mph Grand Tourer built to confront Ferrari head-on. The 2004 Vanquish S raised power to 520bhp. The last Aston built almost entirely by hand at Newport Pagnell before production moved to Gaydon.

generations.name: E60 M5 (2005–2010)
generations.description: The E60 M5 contains the S85 — a 500bhp naturally aspirated V10 derived from the M3 CSL's concept and the Williams F1 programme. Nothing else sounds or feels like it. The Touring estate variant is extraordinarily rare. SMG gearbox requires maintenance attention.

generations.name: 1M Coupe (2011–2012)
generations.description: The 1M Coupe is the last BMW M car built to the original M division philosophy — minimum weight, maximum driver involvement, no compromise. The widened E82 body, S65-inspired suspension, and N54 engine made it quicker around the Nürburgring than the E60 M5. Never officially called M1.

generations.name: C63 AMG W204 (2008–2015)
generations.description: The W204 C63 AMG contained the M156 — a 457bhp naturally aspirated 6.2-litre V8 hand-built by a single AMG technician. The last of the large naturally aspirated AMG V8s before forced induction arrived. The Black Series and Edition 507 are the collector variants.

generations.name: Ford GT (2005)
generations.description: Ford built the 2005 GT to celebrate its centenary and its Le Mans legacy. Hand-laid fibreglass over an aluminium honeycomb chassis, 550bhp supercharged V8, and retro GT40 proportions. Only 4,038 were built — all in the same two years. Values have tripled in a decade.

generations.name: Corvette C5 Z06 (1997–2004)
generations.description: The C5 Z06 transformed the Corvette from a cruise missile into a proper track weapon. The LS6 engine, Bilstein shocks, and titanium exhaust produced a car that humiliated Ferraris at a fraction of the price. Fixed roof coupe only — no convertible Z06.

generations.name: Corvette C6 ZR1 (2009–2013)
generations.description: The C6 ZR1 was the most powerful production Corvette ever made at launch — 638bhp from a supercharged LS9 hand-built at the Corvette engine plant. Carbon ceramic brakes, carbon hood, and a top speed of 205mph. Outran everything at its price point.

generations.name: Viper ACR Gen 3 (2008–2010)
generations.description: The ACR — American Club Racer — is the Viper distilled to its most extreme. Standard aero package produces 1,000lb of downforce at speed. Set production car lap records at Road America, Laguna Seca, and 13 other circuits. No traction control. No apologies.

generations.name: Shelby GT500 (2007–2014)
generations.engine_options: 5.4 L Supercharged V8,5.8 L Supercharged V8
generations.description: The SVT Shelby GT500 returned the supercharged big-block formula to the Mustang for the first time since the 1960s. The 2013 upgrade to the 5.8-litre Trinity V8 produced 662bhp — briefly the most powerful production V8 in the world. Glass roof option unique to this generation.

generations.name: Lancer Evolution IX (2005–2007)
generations.description: The Evo IX was the final chapter of the 4G63-powered Evo era — the engine that defined the nameplate. The MR (Mitsubishi Racing) variant with twin-clutch SST previewed the future; the RS with manual gearbox preserved the past. The last Evo worth arguing about.

generations.name: Impreza WRX STI GD (2001–2007)
generations.description: The GD chassis brought the STI to the US market for the first time in 2004. The Blobeye (2004–05) and Hawkeye (2006–07) facelifts are the collector targets. The R205 and S204 Japanese-market specials are extraordinarily rare.

generations.name: Veyron (2005–2011)
generations.description: The Veyron was the first production car to break 1,000bhp and 400km/h. Its W16 engine with four turbochargers required ten radiators and a seven-speed dual-clutch gearbox. Engineering excess as art. The Super Sport raised the bar to 1,200bhp and 268mph.

generations.name: 996 GT3 RS (2006–2009)
generations.description: The 997 GT3 RS brought the GT3's motorsport DNA to its most extreme road expression. Wider body, coilover suspension, and the choice of 3.6 or 3.8-litre naturally aspirated flat-sixes. The GT3 RS 4.0 — last air-cooled-style Porsche engine — is the ultimate.

generations.name: RS4 B7 (2006–2008)
generations.description: The B7 RS4 is the definitive RS4 — a naturally aspirated 4.2-litre V8 producing 420bhp, quattro all-wheel drive, and a six-speed manual gearbox. The Avant estate is the understated Q-car par excellence. Porsche-designed suspension, motorsport-derived engine.

generations.name: 166 MM (1948–1953)
generations.description: The 166 MM is the car that established Ferrari's legend. Barchetta (little boat) bodywork by Touring, a 2.0-litre V12, and outright victories at Le Mans and the Mille Miglia in 1949. Every surviving example is a cornerstone of automotive history.

generations.name: 250 GT SWB (1959–1962)
generations.description: The 250 GT Short Wheelbase Berlinetta is the ultimate dual-purpose Ferrari — beautiful enough for the road, fast enough to win Le Mans GT class outright. Stirling Moss drove one at Goodwood. Steel and alloy body versions exist; the alloy competition cars are the most valuable.

generations.name: 250 GT Cabriolet (1957–1962)
generations.description: The 250 GT Cabriolet Series I and II were Pininfarina's open interpretation of the 250 GT. The Series II of 1959 onward is the more refined and collectible car. The California Spyder — open headlight version — is among the most desirable Ferraris ever made.

generations.name: 410 Superamerica (1956–1959)
generations.description: The 410 Superamerica was Ferrari's most powerful and exclusive road car of the 1950s. A 4.9-litre V12, coachbuilt body by Pininfarina or Boano, and a price three times that of a contemporary 250 GT. Built exclusively for wealthy American clients.

generations.name: 365 GTC/4 (1971–1972)
generations.description: The 365 GTC/4 was Ferrari's 2+2 companion to the Daytona. Five-speed gearbox, four overhead camshafts, and side-draught carburettors under a long bonnet. Pininfarina's wedge design was ahead of its time. Only 500 built in just two years.

The 400 and 412 were Ferrari's grand touring 2+2 — the only Ferraris ever offered with an automatic gearbox as standard. Unloved for decades, they are now recognised as supremely elegant Pininfarina designs. Manual examples command significant premiums.

generations.name: 308 GT4 (1973–1980)
generations.description: The 308 GT4 was the first mid-engine 2+2 Ferrari and the only Ferrari road car designed by Bertone rather than Pininfarina. Initially sold as a Dino without Ferrari badging. Its angular Bertone wedge shape divided opinion on launch; today it is recognised as a design masterpiece and significantly undervalued relative to its 308 GTB sibling.

generations.name: Mondial (1980–1993)
generations.description: The Mondial was Ferrari's long-running 2+2 mid-engine car — the only mid-engine Ferrari with a proper rear seat and a convertible option. The Mondial t with transverse gearbox is the most usable; the Cabriolet the most sought after. Extremely accessible entry into Ferrari ownership.

The 348 replaced the 328 and introduced longitudinal engine mounting and a straked side treatment echoing the Testarossa. Initially criticised for wayward handling, late cars with revised suspension are rewarding drivers. The TB and TS are the hardtop variants; the Spider the rarest.

The 456 was Ferrari's return to the front-engine 2+2 after the 412. A 5.5-litre V12, Pininfarina design of extraordinary elegance, and — uniquely — a manual gearbox option that commands large premiums over the automatic. The last great front-engine 2+2 of the classic era.

generations.name: 550 Maranello (1996–2001)
generations.description: The 550 Maranello marked Ferrari's return to the front-engine supercar after 23 years of mid-engine flagships. 485bhp V12, manual gearbox, and a top speed of 199mph. The Barchetta Pininfarina concept spawned a 448-unit open version. The 575M that followed added power and F1 paddle shift.

generations.name: 575M Maranello (2002–2006)
generations.description: The 575M evolved the 550 with 515bhp, updated suspension, and the option of Ferrari's F1 paddle-shift transmission alongside the traditional manual. The Superamerica introduced a unique rotating glass roof — one of the most innovative open-car solutions ever engineered.

generations.name: F430 (2004–2009)
generations.description: The F430 replaced the 360 and raised the bar dramatically — 483bhp, E-Diff electronic differential, and a 0-100mph time under 10 seconds. The F430 Challenge race car is closely related. The Spider with its electrohydraulic roof is the open-air choice.

generations.name: 458 Italia (2009–2015)
generations.description: The 458 Italia is widely regarded as the finest Ferrari of the modern era — a naturally aspirated 570bhp V8 revving to 9,000rpm, double-wishbone suspension, and aerodynamics developed in Formula 1. The Speciale and Speciale A are the stripped track variants. The last naturally aspirated V8 Ferrari.

generations.name: F12 Berlinetta (2012–2017)
generations.description: The F12 Berlinetta produced 730bhp from its 6.3-litre V12 — the most powerful naturally aspirated V12 Ferrari road car. 0-62mph in 3.1 seconds. The TDF (Tour de France) limited edition is the stripped lightweight variant, producing 780bhp with passive aerodynamics. The last of the classic front-engine V12 lineage.

generations.name: LaFerrari (2013–2016)
generations.description: LaFerrari combined a 6.3-litre V12 with a Formula 1-derived hybrid system to produce 950bhp — more than any road car Ferrari had previously made. The HY-KERS system harvested energy under braking. 499 coupes and 210 Apertas were built, each allocated to established Ferrari clients.

generations.name: CR-X Si (1983–1991)
generations.engine_options: 1.5 L ZC I4,1.6 L B16A VTEC I4
generations.description: The CR-X Si is the definitive 1980s lightweight hot hatch. Short wheelbase, near 50/50 weight distribution, and Honda's VTEC engine in late examples made it a giant-killer. The EF8 Si-R with 150bhp VTEC B16A is the collector target — fun, light, and increasingly rare.

generations.name: Civic Type R EK9 (1997–2000)
generations.description: The EK9 Civic Type R was the first Honda to wear the Type R badge. The B16B is the highest-revving naturally aspirated engine Honda ever fitted to a road car — 185bhp from 1.6 litres, redline at 8,200rpm. Championship White only in Japan. Becoming very collectible.

generations.name: Civic Type R EP3 (2001–2005)
generations.description: The EP3 was the first Civic Type R built in the UK and the first to use the K20 engine. Heavier than the EK9 but significantly more powerful at 197bhp. The independent rear suspension transformed cornering balance. Red interior, bucket seats, and close-ratio six-speed standard.

generations.name: Civic Type R FN2 (2007–2011)
generations.description: The FN2 is the last naturally aspirated Civic Type R and the most controversial — the aggressive styling divided opinion. Underneath, the K20 engine, close-ratio gearbox, and front limited-slip differential make it a fine driver's car. The last of the high-revving VTEC Type Rs.

generations.name: Prelude BB6/BB8 (1996–2001)
generations.engine_options: 2.0 L F20B DOHC I4,2.2 L H22A VTEC I4
generations.description: The fifth-generation Prelude was Honda's most technically sophisticated coupe — available with Active Torque Transfer System (ATTS) that actively distributed torque between front wheels for neutral cornering. The H22A VTEC engine produces 200bhp. The last and finest Prelude.

generations.name: Beat (1991–1996)
generations.description: The Honda Beat is Japan's most collectible kei roadster. Mid-engine, rear-drive, naturally aspirated, and with a five-speed gearbox — a tiny Mazda Miata philosophy in miniature. Designed by Pininfarina, produced for only five years. Appreciating rapidly as JDM collector cars cross the 25-year rule.

generations.name: Accord Type R (1998–2002)
generations.description: The Accord Type R is one of the rarest and most overlooked Honda performance cars. Just 3,602 were built, all in Championship White. The H22A7 produces 212bhp — only available with a close-ratio six-speed manual. Front limited-slip differential and Brembo brakes standard.

generations.name: NSX-R GT (2005)
generations.description: Just five NSX-R GTs were built for Super GT racing homologation — each with 600bhp, sequential gearbox, full aero package, and titanium components throughout. Effectively a fully developed racing NSX with number plates.

generations.name: AE86 Corolla (1983–1987)
generations.description: The AE86 is the most culturally significant Japanese car ever made — 'Initial D' made it a global icon, but the reality is even better. Rear-wheel drive, 128bhp twin-cam, and a chassis of perfect simplicity. Trueno (pop-up headlights) versus Levin (fixed) is the great debate. Unmodified survivors are extraordinarily rare.

generations.name: Celica GT-Four ST165 (1985–1989)
generations.description: The ST165 was Toyota's first all-wheel drive Celica and their first WRC competitor. Juha Kankkunen won the 1990 WRC drivers championship in the closely related ST185, but the ST165 laid the groundwork. Group A homologation required 5,000 road cars — all are desirable.

generations.name: Celica GT-Four ST185 (1989–1994)
generations.description: The ST185 won the WRC manufacturers title in 1993 and 1994 with Carlos Sainz and Didier Auriol. The road car matched Group A spec with all-wheel drive, viscous LSDs, and intercooled turbo. The Carlos Sainz Limited Edition with 235bhp is the definitive variant.

generations.name: Supra MK3 A70 (1986–1993)
generations.description: The A70 Supra established the model's performance credentials. The twin-turbo 7M-GTE produces 232bhp and the long bonnet/short deck proportions previewed the legendary A80. The Turbo A is the performance variant. Increasing collector interest as the A80 becomes unaffordable.

generations.name: MR2 AW11 (1984–1989)
generations.description: The AW11 was Toyota's first mid-engine road car and a landmark in affordable sports car design. The supercharged SC version is the performance pick with 145bhp. Pop-up headlights, T-bar roof option, and near-perfect mid-engine balance. The original poor man's Ferrari.

generations.name: MR2 SW20 (1989–1999)
generations.description: The SW20 transformed the MR2 into a genuine supercar rival. The turbocharged 3S-GTE produces 245bhp in later Revision 5 cars. Early snap-oversteer reputation was addressed through three revisions — Revision 5 (1994+) is the definitive car. The Turbo is the collector target.

generations.name: Soarer Z30 / Lexus SC (1991–2000)
generations.description: The Z30 Soarer was Toyota's flagship grand tourer — the 1UZ-FE V8 version sold as the Lexus SC400 in export markets. Electronically controlled air suspension, a V8 whisper-quiet at speed, and elegant 1990s styling. The SC400 with manual swap is the ultimate Japanese GT.

generations.name: Chaser / Mark II JZX90/100 (1992–2001)
generations.description: The JZX90 and JZX100 Chaser and Mark II are the definitive Japanese drift sedans. The 1JZ-GTE twin-turbo inline-six produces 280bhp in stock form and is endlessly tunable. Four-door practicality, rear-wheel drive, and near-infinite power potential. Tourer V is the top spec.

generations.name: Altezza / Lexus IS200 (1998–2005)
generations.description: The Altezza RS200 with the 3S-GE BEAMS engine is the driver's choice — 210bhp, six-speed manual, limited-slip differential. Sold in export markets as the Lexus IS200/IS300. The altezza tail-lights became a 2000s automotive fashion disaster but the car underneath is genuinely good.

generations.name: Land Cruiser 80 (1989–1997)
generations.description: The 80 Series Land Cruiser is the sweet spot of the nameplate — more refined than the FJ40 but without the computer complexity of later generations. Coil springs all round, locking diffs, and a bulletproof drivetrain. The VX Limited with full options is the collector target. Values rising sharply.

generations.name: Bluebird 510 (1967–1973)
generations.description: The 510 Bluebird is Nissan's most significant early road car — the 'Poor Man's BMW 2002' that dominated SCCA sedan racing in America. Rear-wheel drive, independent rear suspension, and twin-cam options made it a genuine sports saloon. Now a cult car in the drift and classic JDM communities.

generations.name: Fairlady Z S130 / 280ZX (1978–1983)
generations.engine_options: 2.8 L L28E I6,2.8 L L28ET Turbo I6
generations.description: The S130 280ZX was a significant commercial success but a departure from the S30's purity. More luxurious, heavier, but the Turbo model offered genuine performance. The 2+2 is the practical choice; the 2-seater Turbo the enthusiast pick. Values rising as S30 prices become prohibitive.

generations.name: Silvia S13 (1988–1994)
generations.engine_options: 1.8 L CA18DET Turbo I4,2.0 L SR20DET Turbo I4
generations.description: The S13 Silvia is the foundation of Japanese drift culture. Lightweight, rear-wheel drive, and with the SR20DET engine producing 205bhp in stock form — endlessly tunable to 500bhp+. The 180SX hatchback sibling shares the platform. The 240SX in North America used the same body with different engine.

generations.name: Silvia S14 (1993–1998)
generations.engine_options: 2.0 L SR20DE I4,2.0 L SR20DET Turbo I4
generations.description: The S14 grew the Silvia into a more complete package — wider track, better aero, and refined SR20DET. The NISMO-tuned 270RS and Autech versions are the collector targets. The Kouki (late) facelifted front end is more aggressive. Still the benchmark affordable RWD drift platform.

generations.name: Silvia S15 (1999–2002)
generations.engine_options: 2.0 L SR20DE I4,2.0 L SR20DET Turbo I4
generations.description: The S15 was the final Silvia and never officially sold in North America — making it the most desirable for US collectors under the 25-year import rule. Sharper styling, improved suspension, and optional six-speed Getrag gearbox. The Spec-R Aero with 250bhp is the ultimate S15.

generations.name: Nissan GT-R R35 (2007–2022)
generations.description: The R35 GT-R shocked the automotive world in 2007 — a production car lapping the Nürburgring in 7:29, outrunning cars costing twice the price. The dual-clutch transmission launches it to 60mph in 2.7 seconds. Nismo and Track Edition variants are the collector targets. Brutally quick, endlessly tuneable.

generations.name: 350Z Z33 (2002–2009)
generations.engine_options: 3.5 L VQ35DE V6,3.5 L VQ35HR V6
generations.description: The 350Z revived the Z-car formula after the 300ZX was discontinued — rear-wheel drive, V6, affordable, and properly sporting. The Track and NISMO variants are the performance picks. The Roadster is the open-air choice. Now entering the zone where clean examples attract serious collectors.

generations.name: 370Z Z34 (2008–2021)
generations.description: The 370Z refined the 350Z with a shorter wheelbase, more power, and SynchroRev Match for perfect heel-and-toe downshifts. The NISMO variant with 350bhp and Rays wheels is the collector pick. The last of the classic Z-car lineage before the Z (RZ34).

generations.name: Stagea WC34 (1996–2001)
generations.engine_options: 2.5 L RB25DET Turbo I6,2.5 L RB26DETT Twin-Turbo I6
generations.description: The Stagea WC34 Autech 260RS is the ultimate Q-car — a practical five-door estate with the complete GT-R drivetrain including the twin-turbo RB26DETT and ATTESA E-TS all-wheel drive. Just 1,000 260RS cars were built. Grocery runs at 150mph have never been more subtle.

generations.name: Silver Ghost (1906–1926)
generations.description: The Silver Ghost earned its name from its near-silent running and silver paintwork — the original 40/50hp was the first car called 'the best car in the world' by the motoring press. Coachbuilt on a bare chassis, no two are identical. The 1907 London-to-Edinburgh trial proved its reliability. Among the most coveted veteran cars at auction.

generations.name: Phantom I (1925–1931)
generations.description: The Phantom I succeeded the Silver Ghost with a new overhead-valve engine and central gearchange. Coachbuilt bodies by the finest coachbuilders — Barker, Hooper, Park Ward, Brewster in America. Lawrence of Arabia owned one. Every surviving example is individually documented.

generations.name: Phantom II (1929–1936)
generations.description: The Phantom II introduced a new low-slung chassis that enabled more dramatic coachwork. The Continental version with short wheelbase and sporting body is the most desirable. Maharajas and royalty were the primary clientele. Barker and Gurney Nutting bodies are the most sought-after.

generations.name: Phantom III (1936–1940)
generations.description: The Phantom III was the first Rolls-Royce V12 and the last pre-war Phantom. Independent front suspension was a technical landmark. Only 727 were completed before the war halted production. Each body was unique — Gurney Nutting, Windovers, and H.J. Mulliner produced the finest examples.

generations.name: Silver Wraith (1946–1959)
generations.description: The Silver Wraith was the first post-war Rolls-Royce, sold as a bare chassis for coachbuilding until 1955. Park Ward, H.J. Mulliner, and James Young produced the finest bodies. Long Wheelbase versions are the stateliest. The last Rolls-Royce sold exclusively as a chassis for coachwork.

generations.name: Silver Cloud I/II/III (1955–1965)
generations.description: The Silver Cloud is the definitive post-war Rolls-Royce shape — Rolls's first standard steel body designed in-house. The Silver Cloud II introduced the 6.2-litre V8; the III added quad headlamps. Convertible versions by Park Ward are among the most beautiful post-war British cars. The James Young two-door is exceptionally rare.

generations.name: Silver Shadow I/II (1965–1980)
generations.description: The Silver Shadow was the most radical Rolls-Royce in decades — unibody construction, four-wheel disc brakes, independent rear suspension. The most common Rolls-Royce ever made, which suppressed values for years. Now rising as condition examples become scarce. Two-door drophead coupe is the most desirable body style.

generations.name: Corniche (1971–1995)
generations.description: The Corniche convertible is the most glamorous post-war Rolls-Royce — and one of the longest-running models in automotive history at 24 years. Built by Mulliner Park Ward on the Silver Shadow platform. The Corniche S and final Series V with fuel injection are the most sophisticated. A Riviera staple.

generations.name: Silver Spirit / Silver Spur (1980–1999)
generations.description: The Silver Spirit updated the Silver Shadow's platform with contemporary styling, improved air conditioning, and from 1991 an electronic self-levelling suspension. The long-wheelbase Silver Spur is the chauffeur choice. The Silver Spirit III and Touring Limousine are the final refinements before the Silver Seraph.

generations.name: Silver Seraph (1998–2002)
generations.description: The Silver Seraph was the first BMW-era Rolls-Royce — its 5.4-litre V12 was sourced from BMW's 750iL. The handbuilt body retained the traditional upright grille and classic proportions. Just 2,138 were made before the all-new Phantom arrived. The transition car between old and new Rolls-Royce.

generations.name: Phantom VII (2003–2016)
generations.description: The seventh-generation Phantom re-established Rolls-Royce as the world's pre-eminent luxury car under BMW ownership. Spaceframe aluminium construction, a 460bhp V12, and a rear-hinged coach door. The Drophead Coupe and Coupe variants are particularly collectible. Bespoke commissions through the Rolls-Royce Private Office command extraordinary premiums.

generations.name: Model K (1931–1942)
generations.description: The Lincoln Model K was America's finest coachbuilt car of the 1930s — a V12-powered platform bodied by Brunn, Judkins, LeBaron, and Willoughby into some of the most dramatic American automobiles ever made. Franklin D. Roosevelt's parade car was a Model K. The KB with the 7.0-litre V12 is the ultimate expression.

generations.name: Continental Mk I (1940–1942)
generations.description: The 1940 Lincoln Continental is considered by many automotive historians the most beautiful American car ever designed. Edsel Ford sketched it himself as a personal car while vacationing in Florida. The cabriolet with its razor-edge styling, continental spare tyre, and low roofline set a standard that influenced decades of American car design.

generations.name: Cosmopolitan (1949–1951)
generations.description: The Cosmopolitan was Lincoln's post-war statement of intent — a full-size luxury car competing directly with Cadillac. The convertible is extraordinarily rare. Lincoln finished second through fifth at the 1950 Pan-American Road Race with Cosmopolitans, establishing the nameplate's performance credibility.

generations.name: Capri / Premiere (1952–1957)
generations.description: The Capri and its successor Premiere represented Lincoln at its most elegant in the classic American era. The 1956-57 Premiere Convertible is one of the most handsome American open cars. Lincoln swept the top four positions in the 1952 Pan-American Road Race with production Capris.

generations.name: Continental Mk II (1956–1957)
generations.description: The Continental Mark II was America's most expensive production car when launched at $10,000 — nearly twice the price of a Cadillac Eldorado. Each was hand-built to order over 14 days on its own assembly line. Rust-proofed, individually matched panels, and personally inspected by company executives. A near-perfect American luxury coupe.

generations.name: Continental (1961–1969)
generations.description: The 1961 Lincoln Continental is the most significant American car of the 1960s — four-door convertible with rear-hinged suicide doors, pure rectangular lines, and no unnecessary ornamentation. Elwood Engel designed it while at Chrysler; it won the IDSA Industrial Design Award. JFK rode in a stretched version in Dallas on November 22, 1963.

generations.name: Continental Mk III / IV / V (1968–1979)
generations.description: The Mark III was Lincoln's answer to the Ford Thunderbird personal luxury coupe. Its neo-classic styling with fake spare tyre hump proved enormously popular. The Mark IV and V followed with growing dimensions. Elvis Presley famously owned multiple examples. The Mark V Bill Blass Edition is the most collectible.

generations.name: Town Car (1980–2011)
generations.engine_options: 5.0 L V8,4.6 L V8,4.6 L V8 SOHC
generations.description: The Town Car was Lincoln's mainstream flagship for three decades — the default American limousine base car, black-car staple, and retirement community favourite. The 1998–2002 Cartier Edition is the most complete; the final 2011 cars the most refined. Now rising as a long-wheelbase American classic of the late 20th century.

generations.name: Mark VIII (1993–1998)
generations.description: The Mark VIII is the last great Lincoln coupe — a sleek, aluminium-intensive body over an air-ride suspension and a 280bhp 4.6-litre DOHC V8. The 1997-98 LSC in black or white are the collector targets. Dramatically undervalued relative to its engineering and styling achievement.

generations.name: Navigator 1st Gen (1997–2003)
generations.description: The first Navigator created the American luxury SUV segment when it launched in 1997 and outsold the Cadillac Escalade for years. The 2003 Blackwood pickup variant is exceptionally rare. Early examples are now entering collector interest as defining artefacts of late 1990s American culture.

generations.name: 600 Grosser (1963–1981)
generations.description: The 600 Grosser was the most technically ambitious car in the world when launched — a hydraulically operated everything: windows, seats, sunroof, boot lid, doors. At 5.5 metres and nearly 2.5 tonnes, it was the choice of heads of state, royalty, and dictators. Elvis, Coco Chanel, John Lennon, and Mao Zedong all owned one. The Landaulet is the rarest and most desirable body style.

generations.name: SL R107 (1971-1985)
generations.description: The R107 SL is the longest-running Mercedes model in history at 18 years. Sold as the 350SL through to the 560SL, it is the definitive open Mercedes grand tourer. The 560SL is the most powerful and the American collector favourite. Hardtop and soft top supplied as standard on all cars.

generations.name: W108 / W109 (1965–1972)
generations.description: The W108 and long-wheelbase W109 are the S-Class that established Mercedes flagship supremacy. The 300SEL 6.3 — stuffed with the 600's V8 — was the fastest four-door sedan in the world in 1968. A German muscle car in a suit. The 300SEL 6.3 is the collector target; standard 280SE the accessible entry.

generations.name: 190E 2.3-16 / 2.5-16 (1983–1993)
generations.engine_options: 2.3 L Cosworth I4,2.5 L Cosworth I4
generations.description: The 190E 2.3-16 was developed with Cosworth — a 16-valve cylinder head on Mercedes' small sedan. Launched with a race at the Nürburgring where Ayrton Senna beat Niki Lauda. The Evolution I and Evolution II are homologation specials for DTM racing, with just 502 and 500 built respectively. The Evo II with its dramatic rear wing is the most desirable.

generations.name: 300CE / E36 AMG (1987–1993)
generations.description: The W124 Coupe is the finest everyday Mercedes ever made — understated, beautifully built, and with the optional 3.6-litre AMG engine, genuinely fast. The 300CE-24 with 24-valve head and the E36 AMG (3.6-litre) are the collector picks. The Cabriolet is the most elegant open Mercedes of the era.

generations.name: SL R129 (1989–2001)
